/uk-news/2026/oct/31/uk-police-should-no.headline: US military failed to notify UK police of drink-driving allegation against airman based in England
/uk-news/2026/oct/31/uk-police-should-no.excerpt: The US military failed to notify British police of an allegation that one of its airmen had been drink-driving in Suffolk, preventing the British authorities from being able to investigate the offence. The failure broke a longstanding formal agreement with British police that enables the UK to investigate alleged illegality by US military personnel who are stationed in Britain. The airman, Christopher Mooty, had spent the night drinking with two other American service personnel in a market town before driving them to buy a kebab in the early hours of the morning. The allegation of drink-driving was later reported to his commanders, who then used their own internal processes to discipline him. The case raises questions over how many other US military personnel based in the UK have committed crimes that have not been flagged to British police forces. Mooty went on to commit a second drink-driving offence a year later. This time he was prosecuted in a British court. The latest disclosures are part of the Guardian’s investigation into crimes carried out by American military personnel who are based in Britain. The series prompted the UK government and police chiefs to set up a high-level inquiry in the summer to establish whether US military personnel stationed in Britain are being brought to justice properly. In the latest case, Mooty, then a 21-year-old airman working at the huge United States Air Force (USAF) base at Mildenhall, Suffolk, went on a night out in March 2023.
/uk-news/2026/oct/31/uk-police-should-no.trail: British authorities were unable to investigate case of Christopher Mooty, who went on to commit another offence

/world/2026/oct/31/police-clash-rioters-.headline: Cost of living protests  to spread to Germany and reignite in France on Halloween
/world/2026/oct/31/police-clash-rioters-.excerpt: Street protests sweeping Europe are expected to spread to Germany and reignite in France on Saturday, with police mobilised to stop potential looting and rioting on the fringes of what organisers hope will be peaceful rallies. Weeks of, at times violent, student demonstrations have rocked Italy, Spain, Portugal, Albania and France, where activists on Halloween have again called for people to make their anger over the cost of living and deficient public services felt across the country. In Germany, a loose alliance of groups called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z is sorting it) has called for supporters to turn out in more than 30 cities demanding more spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and against any plans to return to mandatory military service. Alexander Throm, of the ruling conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) parliamentary group, wrote in the Handelsblatt business newspaper: “Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs.” But Felix Banaszak, the co-leader of the opposition Green party, cautioned against attempts to place the youth protests under general suspicion in advance. “The [CDU’s] rhetoric, which seeks to criminalise these protests pre-emptively and paint them as the work of marauding gangs, may even drive people towards radicalisation,” he told the RND media group.
/world/2026/oct/31/police-clash-rioters-.trail: Activists call for people to make their anger known over poor public services including education and housing

/world/2026/oct/31/police-clash-rioters-.headline: Protest leaders urge French pupils to keep barricading their schools
/world/2026/oct/31/police-clash-rioters-.excerpt: French children should continue to barricade their schools and take part in street protests, a student union said on Monday after the government announced a package of education measures to try to stem the crisis. “Today we’re at the negotiating table, we’re able to negotiate with the government,” Pierre Sourzat of Les Lycéens told France Info television. “We’re in a power struggle and we still need to call for continued mobilisation to meet a maximum of our demands.” The government told high school student representatives it would cap some class sizes and review the university application system. But Sourzat said: “We want measures, not half measures.” More than five weeks after the start of high school blockades in September, the government made the proposals to address the demands of what has become the biggest youth protest movement in years. It has been joined by trade unions and cost-of-living protesters in regular mass street demonstrations on Saturdays. High school pupils had demanded an end to teacher and staff shortages and for repairs to decrepit school buildings that had collapsing ceilings, mould, broken toilets, a lack of chairs and windows that did not shut. The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said some schools were so dilapidated they were “not fit” for teaching. He announced a government loan of €4bn to regional authorities to begin repairs.
/world/2026/oct/31/police-clash-rioters-.trail: Activists say struggle must go on until their ‘maximum’ demands are met over teacher shortages and building repairs

/world/2026/oct/31/police-clash-rioters-.headline: Macron accused of putting France’s right to protest at risk with ‘vandal’s law’
/world/2026/oct/31/police-clash-rioters-.excerpt: Emmanuel Macron has been accused by trade unions of trying to curb the fundamental French right to protest as the government fast-tracks a bill to make protesters pay for damage caused by vandalism at street demonstrations even if they did not directly cause it themselves. The French president, who leaves office next spring, has faced more than a month of protests in which high-school students have blockaded schools demanding a response to teacher absences, repairs to decrepit buildings and changes to the university applications platform. Trade unions and gilets jaunes (yellow vest) anti-government protesters are now joining sustained street demonstrations in a growing social crisis over schools, as well as the cost of living and public services. Authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrating after France saw one of its worst days of violence in years earlier this month when largely peaceful demonstrations were marred by looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings. The senate will this week debate the government’s proposed “vandals pay” law. The legislation would mean that a person protesting could be held liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage and vandalism even if they did not directly cause it themselves, if they were continuing to demonstrate nearby or as part of the same group as perpetrators. The bill also provides for greater use of drones over protests.
/world/2026/oct/31/police-clash-rioters-.trail: Making innocent protesters liable for damage would be bad for rule of law and play into far-right hands, say opponents

/world/2026/oct/31/police-clash-rioters-.headline: Hundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policing
/world/2026/oct/31/police-clash-rioters-.excerpt: Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president. The prosecutor’s office in the southern city of Nice said on Sunday that 59 people had been taken into police custody, including 11 suspected of belonging to extreme-right groups. They were alleged to have gathered with the intent of committing violence. Some were arrested in two vehicles with masks, gloves, gas sprays and truncheons, the prosecutor’s office said in a statement to public broadcaster FranceInfo. Local media in Nice had reported extreme-right groups coming to the city centre and targeting demonstrators on Saturday. In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates. They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions. The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”.
/world/2026/oct/31/police-clash-rioters-.trail: Almost 1,000 arrested as police charge crowd in Paris and teargas used to stop protesters reaching other city centres

/world/2026/oct/31/police-clash-rioters-.headline: France to deploy 70,000 police on Saturday to prevent civil unrest
/world/2026/oct/31/police-clash-rioters-.excerpt: France will deploy about 70,000 police around the country on Saturday as the government seeks to prevent more civil unrest after some of the worst street violence in years erupted on the fringes of cost-of-living protests last weekend. The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on ⁠Friday ⁠the security forces would include elite units usually used for counter-terrorism operations and hostage rescues, adding that there had been social media calls for violence from “ultra-left” groups. “We are not talking about ⁠a peaceful, friendly demonstration,” Nuñez told reporters after a meeting of senior ministers and officials chaired by the president, Emmanuel Macron. “We are ready tomorrow to be ‌extremely firm and not tolerate anything.” Major museums including the Louvre, Orsay Museum, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais – where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display – are closed Saturday. Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organisers to cancel the weekend program. Parisian shopkeepers have been barricading their stores all week. Near Place de la République in Paris, one of last weekend’s hotspots, a bank branch and other businesses were boarded up with wooden panels to deter potential looters. Macron and his government are struggling to get on top of a crisis that has caught it off guard six months before presidential elections to choose his successor.
/world/2026/oct/31/police-clash-rioters-.trail: Security forces to include elite units usually used for counter-terrorism after worst street violence in years

/uk-news/2026/oct/31/man-belfast-charged.headline: Fancy a pint … at Lidl? The bizarre battle over Northern Ireland’s stifled nightlife
/uk-news/2026/oct/31/man-belfast-charged.excerpt: At first sight The Middle Ale in Dundonald, Northern Ireland looks just like any other pub. There is a big TV, an array of seating, and beer pumps behind the bar. Look a little closer, however, and you might ask why there are packets of fajitas and gravy granules on the walls. That’s because the pub belongs to the supermarket chain Lidl, but the Middle Ale (like “middle aisle”, get it?) isn’t just a wacky marketing stunt. Northern Ireland has ultra-strict laws around licences to sell alcohol, whether as a shop, pub or nightclub. Lidl tried to get a licence to sell alcohol in its Dundonald store, and was refused, but after a court battle it did manage to get a licence for a pub – which it duly opened next door, selling alcohol to take away as well as serving drinks in the pub itself. It’s an absurd chapter of a much bigger story: local activists have long demanded licensing reform that could invigorate Northern Irish nightlife. The Lidl pub situation exposed “the hypocrisy of everything we’re up against,” says Boyd Sleator. In 2021, Sleator and Belfast-based DJ Holly Lester co-founded Free the Night, a charitable organisation formed in 2021 with the aim of creating a safe and progressive nightlife in Northern Ireland. Research conducted by Free the Night claims that obtaining an alcohol licence in Northern Ireland costs, on average, £75,250, but they say they have heard of sums up to £1m changing hands.
/uk-news/2026/oct/31/man-belfast-charged.trail: The country’s licensing laws mean the supermarket has opened a pub so it can sell alcohol, while campaigners are fighting to help other venues open and get people dancing

/uk-news/2026/oct/31/man-belfast-charged.headline: Belfast teenager whose body was found in storm drain ‘failed by the PSNI’
/uk-news/2026/oct/31/man-belfast-charged.excerpt: An inquest into the death of a teenager whose body was found in a Belfast storm drain has found there is not enough evidence to explain the puzzling circumstances of how he died, partly because of mistakes by police investigators. Noah Donohoe, 14, was last seen on 21 June 2020 when he left his south Belfast home on his bicycle, telling his mother he was going to visit friends. His naked body was found six days later, deep inside an underground water tunnel in the north of the city. The case provoked huge interest in Northern Ireland, with intense speculation on social media over how and why he died, and concerns raised about the police handling of the case. A postmortem in 2020 found that Noah died by drowning. The inquest jury had heard witness and CCTV evidence that Noah had been seen cycling through Belfast in the afternoon and early evening of Sunday 21 June, at one point falling from his bike, and apparently abandoning items of clothing and possessions as he went. He was eventually seen cycling naked, and was captured on CCTV abandoning his black Apollo mountain bike and making his way in the direction of a stream that led to the storm drain. A jury at Belfast coroners’ court found no failings by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) that might have contributed to the teenager’s death. However, they identified a series of 13 failures by investigators that they said had affected their ability to reach conclusions on its circumstances.
/uk-news/2026/oct/31/man-belfast-charged.trail: Not enough evidence to explain circumstances of Noah Donohoe’s death, partly due to police mistakes, inquest finds

/uk-news/2026/oct/31/man-belfast-charged.headline: Most X accounts posting about Belfast and Southampton unrest were based outside UK
/uk-news/2026/oct/31/man-belfast-charged.excerpt: More than half the accounts that posted on Elon Musk’s X about the rioting in Belfast and the civil disorder in Southampton in June were based outside the UK, an analysis by the Guardian can reveal. Of the 8,672 accounts whose combined posts about the events exceeded 1,000 views, just 45.3% were shown as from the UK, according to the social media platform’s own location function. One in six (16.8%) came from the US, 4.5% from Ireland, and about a quarter from all European countries other than the UK. Seven of the 12 most-read tweets about Belfast and Southampton came from the US – including one from Musk himself and two other US “alt-right” commentators – while an eighth was linked to North America. The analysis underlines that US rightwing actors are seeking to influence the UK and boost their position on X in moments of disorder – an exploitation of flashpoint events that has only intermittently attracted political attention in Britain. Nearly a third of all 43,000 posts on X relating to the two incidents contained racist or anti-immigration comments. Almost one in 10 relating to Belfast contained calls for violence or paramilitary or vigilante action. Imran Ahmed, the chief executive of the Centre for Countering Digital Hate, said the data demonstrated that X had become “a weapon of choice” for hostile foreign actors seeking to manipulate shocking and divisive content.
/uk-news/2026/oct/31/man-belfast-charged.trail: Exclusive: Analysis shows 55% of accounts were overseas – and seven of 12 most-read posts came from US

/politics/2026/oct/31/streeting-stockpil.headline: Every Briton should stockpile water and food supplies, government advises
/politics/2026/oct/31/streeting-stockpil.excerpt: Every Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in new government guidance designed to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency. The Be Ready campaign is aimed at persuading people to stock up with supplies to last 72 hours, amid growing official concern about the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats. Dan Jarvis, the security minister, said that “those who can follow this advice should follow this advice”. It amounted to “simple steps to be ready for everyday emergencies” as part of a wider, community-oriented effort “to improve our resilience as a nation”, he said. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, added that Britain also needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure. “Terms like ‘hybrid warfare’ and ‘grey zone threats’ do not accurately capture or convey to the general public what I prefer to describe as ‘state-sponsored terrorism’,” he said. “So in the face of those threats, which are not hypothetical but real, and not somewhere else but increasingly here, we have to step up and take seriously our national resilience as well as our national defence. “It’s really important that we ask households and businesses, are they prepared? Are they ready?
/politics/2026/oct/31/streeting-stockpil.trail: Be Ready campaign aims to prepare UK for impact of climate crisis, technological dependency and threats by hostile state

/politics/2026/oct/31/streeting-stockpil.headline: Race to rearm: Telford gun hall brings tank barrel production back to the UK
/politics/2026/oct/31/streeting-stockpil.excerpt: For the last 20 years, Britain was unable to put a barrel on its tanks without buying from abroad. Relying on foreign allies seemed like a reasonable choice during years of relative security (for wealthy countries at least) after the end of the cold war. But Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has changed the calculation – and prompted a scramble to rearm among European countries, including the UK. Evidence of that scramble was on display on Thursday in Shropshire, where the UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, opened a factory hastily constructed by Germany’s Rheinmetall to make barrels for artillery and British tanks. Such was the urgency that Rheinmetall’s chief executive, Armin Papperger, said the company had started investment “off the back of a handshake” before Christmas last year with Gen Sir Roly Walker, who leads the British army as chief of the general staff, without waiting for a formal contract. Eight months later, production of the first barrels at the factory in Telford has started. Papperger said he was in talks to produce more ammunition in the UK as well, with a decision due in the next six to eight months. Streeting said: “It is not enough to simply out-innovate those who would wish us harm – though we must. We must also out-produce them too.
/politics/2026/oct/31/streeting-stockpil.trail: Defence secretary says Britain must manufacture at scale as Germany’s Rheinmetall opens Midlands factory

/politics/2026/oct/31/streeting-stockpil.headline: Streeting delays defence jobs plan for young people after union pushback
/politics/2026/oct/31/streeting-stockpil.excerpt: Wes Streeting has been forced to delay the publication of a plan to get more young people into defence industry jobs after pushback from trade unions, the Guardian understands. The defence secretary had been due to announce the proposals on Thursday, but some unions in the sector are understood to have reacted angrily to the plans, accusing the government of bypassing their members and minimising their roles in job creation. The delay risks derailing a planned series of government announcements to tackle the youth jobs crisis, with ministers stating on Monday that jobs plans in business services, construction, technology and defence would be published this week. Streeting is expected to visit Telford on Thursday to unveil a major new gun production facility run by German defence giant Rheinmetall, after promising that the defence jobs plan would “help deliver thousands of opportunities for young people, including an increase in the number of people supported through apprenticeship programmes in the defence sector to at least 14,000 annually by 2035”. But the Guardian understands that unions representing workers in the sector were shown the plan just before publication, and told ministers that they would not support it, forcing the 11th-hour delay. Sources at the Ministry of Defence (MoD) confirmed the delay, but played down the role of unions in the hold-up, stating there were issues that still had to be worked through, but that it would be published “in due course”.
/politics/2026/oct/31/streeting-stockpil.trail: UK defence secretary had been due to unveil proposals on Thursday until concerns were raised at 11th hour

/politics/2026/oct/31/streeting-stockpil.headline: Wes Streeting urges US to back Ukraine on Washington visit after Starlink row
/politics/2026/oct/31/streeting-stockpil.excerpt: Wes Streeting urged the US to stand by Ukraine on his visit to the American capital and sought to cool tensions between the two countries in the wake of the Starlink row that is threatening to set back Kyiv’s war effort. The British defence secretary, giving a speech before a meeting with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, argued that supporting Ukraine was in the long-term interests of Washington, and a business opportunity. Taking questions after his address, Streeting acknowledged “the challenges of recent days”, a reference to the row over the sudden decision of the US government on Monday to limit the use of Starlink by Ukraine’s military. He said it was “a reminder of two things – one is that American support in Ukraine has been significant and it has made, I think, a real impact in the Ukrainian war effort. And we and the Ukrainians would feel the absence of that.” The second was that there was “an enormous opportunity for the US in terms of the support for Ukraine”, a reference to the future “defence-industrial relationship” between the countries. Streeting was speaking at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US thinktank, before meeting Hegseth amid tensions over Ukraine, Iran and the Middle East. Speaking to the BBC after the meeting, Streeting said he had been “reassured directly” by his US counterpart that access to the vital Starlink communications system had been restored.
/politics/2026/oct/31/streeting-stockpil.trail: UK defence secretary says he has been ‘reassured directly’ by counterpart Pete Hegseth that Starlink system has been restored as he seeks to cool tensions

/politics/2026/oct/31/streeting-stockpil.headline: UK defence contractors to offer 40,000 apprenticeships, placements and jobs
/politics/2026/oct/31/streeting-stockpil.excerpt: Defence contractors have promised to create 40,000 apprenticeships, work experience placements and jobs for young people each year, as Wes Streeting claimed to be overseeing a “ministry for growth”. Labour is keen to demonstrate that the rapid increase in defence spending planned for the coming years, which may necessitate tax rises, will result in jobs in the UK. In particular, Streeting said he was determined the defence industry should play its part in tackling what he called the “moral emergency” of almost 1 million 16-to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neet). “I think we have a responsibility, as we’re investing more in the defence of the realm, to do so in a way that boosts British jobs, British industry, and helps to deal with this moral emergency,” he said. “I want the Ministry of Defence to be a ministry of growth and a ministry of opportunity, and that’s how we’re going to direct our defence spending.” The defence secretary was speaking before a roundtable with leaders from large contractors, including BAE Systems, MDBA and Rolls-Royce. The firms have signed up to a series of pledges aimed at opening up more opportunities for young people. They have promised to offer 40,000 18- to 24-year-olds each year an opportunity in the sector by 2030 – whether via work experience, an apprenticeship or a permanent role. That is scheduled to rise to 50,000 by 2035.
/politics/2026/oct/31/streeting-stockpil.trail: Wes Streeting says he leads a ‘ministry for growth’ as Labour seeks to show more defence spending will create UK jobs
